title: Copying singers; blues, gospel and the roots of jazz
summary: Vocal records, Nat Cole, blues and gospel as roots.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I, myself, copy vocal records as much as I copy instrumental records. And I still will copy a vocal record because of the phrasing and the feeling, the breath control, that kind of thing. And I don't think, in the case of a wind player, that you should limit yourself to jazz players. If you hear a good opera singer, just for phrasing -- I'm talking about a technical point of view, just for phrasing and breath control, listen to a good opera singer or a good popular singer. I have all of Nat Cole's records, I copy his vocals. I like Tony Bennett's way. I love Ella Fitzgerald. I don't like that singing stuff, but the way she sings a melody is really high class. And Dinah Washington I love.

I think people should listen to good blues singers a great deal. If you want to be a jazz player and you don't have a feeling for good blues singers, I think you may as well forget it because you're not going to be a jazz player in the sense that I know what jazz is. So then you've got another branch because just a few inches behind blues singers is the good gospel singing. And if you want your blood to run cold, you listen to somebody sing "God Be With You" or one of those great songs, "Amazing Grace" or something. And your blood

will just run cold.
I hear that in Louie all the time. I never heard him do a really gospel song -- well, 'Nobody Knows the Trouble..' but he didn't do it gospel style. But the way he soars melodically when he plays, it's like a good (inaudible), you know.
And, you know, to play the blues or any of that feeling, you don't have to play the blues, I mean, if you've got feeling, that sound has to be in anything you play.

Jazz came out of three things, I feel. It came out of the marching band, it came out of the religious service, and it came out of the old ballads, Scotch-Irish, black, the whole thing where it all started. How or where it started is not all that important. The point is that those are the three things, so you have the rhythmic feel of the bands because it used to be, you know, that bands played for dancing. Marching bands, there used to be these little marching bands. I think we talked about that, and the players would have to make up their parts. And that's, I think, a lot of how improvisation got started. And the same way with these beautiful songs, the ballads and the gospel songs.
